milestones.title: tool schemas and argument validation
milestones.task: Write validate_args(schema, args) and Registry.definitions(). Supported: required, unexpected arguments, type (string, integer, number, boolean, array, object), enum, minimum, maximum and pattern. The rules for the order of the problems and for bools and floats are in the docstring.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 1 shows this milestone as ✔. It checks the registry (exact keys, order, a fresh list each call), then a dozen hand-written bad calls against the issue_refund schema (one problem each, naming the argument and what would be valid), then sixty seeded random schemas: valid arguments give [], and breaking exactly one thing gives exactly one problem that names it.
milestones.explain:
A tool schema is the contract between the model and your function: a name, a description and an input_schema written in JSON Schema, a standard vocabulary for the shape of a JSON document (which keys exist, their types, which are required, allowed values). The model reads the schema and writes arguments. It does not always follow it. It invents an extra key, sends "25" where an integer belongs, writes 1001 for A-1001, or picks a reason that is not in the list. Treat those arguments exactly as you would treat the body of an HTTP request from the internet: untrusted input, checked before anything runs (the same rule as for any injection).

You will not implement the whole of JSON Schema, which is large. Six features cover almost every real tool: required, unexpected keys, type, enum, minimum and maximum, and pattern. Two details deserve care. In Python, True is an int, so a naive isinstance(value, int) accepts true as an amount of 1 cent. And a pattern must match the whole string: A-10012 is not an order id.

The other half of the milestone is quieter. The list your registry sends as tools= on every request has exactly three keys per tool (name, description, input_schema) and never the Python function. That list is part of every request you send, so its size is a cost you pay on every iteration, a theme of chapter 5 and of Lab 2.

The messages matter as much as the verdicts. A problem is a sentence the model will read and act on, so it names the argument and says what would be valid. Run the solution on a few bad calls (the demo imports from starter; once you have written your version it runs on yours):

from starter import Shop, make_registry, validate_args

schema = make_registry(Shop()).get("issue_refund").input_schema
print(validate_args(schema, {"order_id": "A-1001", "amount_cents": 2500, "reason": "duplicate"}))
bad = {"order_id": "1001", "amount_cents": "25", "reason": "refund", "note": "hi"}
for problem in validate_args(schema, bad):
    print("-", problem)
print(validate_args(schema, {"order_id": "A-1001", "amount_cents": True, "reason": "damaged"}))
[]
- argument 'order_id' = '1001' does not match the pattern A-\d{4}, for example 'A-1001'
- argument 'amount_cents' must be integer, got string ('25')
- argument 'reason' must be one of ['duplicate', 'damaged', 'goodwill'], got 'refund'
- unexpected argument 'note' (valid arguments: order_id, amount_cents, reason)
["argument 'amount_cents' must be integer, got boolean (True)"]

Compare the first and the last problem with what a bare ValidationError would give the model. "Does not match the pattern" with an example is the difference between the model fixing its call and repeating it.
milestones.card:
A tool's schema is a written contract for its arguments: their names, types, which are required and which values are allowed. The model reads it but still writes calls that break it, so the program around the model checks every call first, as it would check a web request from a stranger.

validate_args(schema, args) returns a list of problems, empty when the call is fine. The model reads each problem and acts on it, so each names the argument and says what would be valid: the allowed values, the bound crossed, an example. In Python True is an int, yet a boolean must not pass as an integer, and a pattern (a regex) must match the whole string. Registry.definitions() returns a fresh list holding, for each tool in self._tools, only name, description and input_schema: never the function.

amount_cents: integer, minimum 1, maximum 10000
2500 ok | "2500" string | True boolean | 2.5 float | 0 below 1

Read more: A4 chapter 6, the contract: JSON Schema.

milestones.title: running one tool call
milestones.task: Write run_tool(registry, call, max_result_chars=2000). It takes one tool_use block and returns one tool_result block, and it never raises. The five failure cases and the truncation rule are in the docstring.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 2 shows this milestone as ✔. It runs each failure case and checks the content and that the function did not run when it should not have (a refund is real money), then truncation (kept prefix, a note with both lengths, errors never cut), malformed calls (input missing or None), and sixty seeded random calls, none of which may raise.
milestones.explain:
A tool call can go wrong in five ways, and a harness that raises in any of them throws away the whole conversation so far. Chapter 2 made the point that the model is good at reading an error and often corrects itself on the next turn, so every failure should come back as a tool_result with is_error set. What you write in the message decides whether the next call is a fix or a repeat:

What happenedWhat the model should be toldDid the function run?
The tool name does not existWhich name was unknown and which tools are availableNo
The arguments are invalidEvery problem from validate_args, and that nothing ranNo
The tool raised ToolErrorThe tool's own message, verbatim: it was written for the modelYes
The tool raised anything elseThe tool name and the exception type, not its messageYes
The result is very longThe first part, plus a note saying it was cut, how much was shown and how to narrow itYes

The fourth row is a deliberate choice. A KeyError: 'secret_table' from a database layer tells an attacker who can steer the model something about your system and tells the model nothing useful; the type is enough for the trace, and the model needs a next step, not a stack. The fifth row comes from chapter 5: a silent cut looks to the model like a complete answer, so say that you truncated and what to do about it. Error messages are never truncated; they are the instructions.

Notice also what the invalid-arguments row protects. If the arguments are checked after the call, issue_refund with amount_cents: "all" has already run. The demo below sends five calls, one of them an invalid refund, and prints what ran:

from starter import Shop, make_registry, run_tool

shop = Shop()
registry = make_registry(shop)
calls = [("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}), ("get_order", {"order_id": "A-9999"}),
         ("issue_refund", {"order_id": "A-1001", "amount_cents": "all", "reason": "damaged"}),
         ("refund_everything", {}), ("get_returns_policy", {})]
for i, (name, args) in enumerate(calls):
    r = run_tool(registry, {"type": "tool_use", "id": f"c{i}", "name": name, "input": args}, max_result_chars=100)
    kind = "ERROR" if r["is_error"] else "ok   "
    print(f"{name:18s} {kind} {r['content'][:118]!r}")
print("refunds:", shop.refunds, "| functions that ran:", shop.executed)
get_order          ok    '{"status": "shipped", "total_cents": 4250, "carrier": "UPS"}'
get_order          ERROR "No order with id 'A-9999'. Order ids look like A-1001."
issue_refund       ERROR "Invalid arguments for issue_refund: argument 'amount_cents' must be integer, got string ('all'). Nothing was run. Fix "
refund_everything  ERROR "Unknown tool 'refund_everything'. Available tools: get_order, track_shipment, issue_refund, get_returns_policy. Nothin"
get_returns_policy ok    '1. Items may be returned within 30 days in their original packaging; refunds go to the original paym\n[truncated: showi'
refunds: [] | functions that ran: ['get_order', 'get_order', 'get_returns_policy']

The invalid refund and the unknown tool left refunds: [] and never reached a function; the missing order raised a ToolError whose text is the instruction. The long policy was cut at 100 characters with a note (a smaller limit than the default, to keep the line short).
milestones.card:
A tool call can fail in several ways, and a loop that crashes on one throws away the whole conversation. So every outcome, good or bad, goes back to the model as a result it can read, and a well-written error lets it fix the next call instead of repeating the last.

run_tool(registry, call) takes one tool_use block, the model's request, and returns one result block built with tool_result. It never raises. Look the tool up, check the arguments with validate_args (already written), and only then run the function: a refund with a bad amount must not execute. A ToolError message was written for the model, so pass it on word for word. Any other exception reports only the tool name and the exception type, because its message may expose internals. A cut-off result must say so, since a silent cut looks like a full answer.

get_order "A-9999"          -> error: the tool's own message
issue_refund amount "all"   -> error: invalid arguments, nothing ran
refund_everything           -> error: unknown tool, real ones listed

Read more: A4 chapter 2, when a tool fails.

milestones.title: stopping rules
milestones.task: Write the three methods of LoopGuard: before_model_call() (return None or the reason to stop), after_model_call(usage) and check_calls(calls). The constructor and the Budget dataclass are given.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 3 shows this milestone as ✔. Hand values first (four calls allowed at max_iterations=3 means the fourth is refused; exactly 100 tokens is allowed against a limit of 100, 101 is not; 30 seconds is allowed, 30.5 is not; a different key order is the same call), then the priority order when several limits are exceeded, then sixty seeded random sequences compared with a plain oracle.
milestones.explain:
Left alone, a model may call tools forever: it cannot find the answer, a tool keeps failing, two steps undo each other. The loop needs limits that your code enforces, because a limit the model is asked to respect is a request, not a barrier. LoopGuard holds four of them. It is pure bookkeeping: it never calls a model or a tool, which is what makes it easy to test exactly.

LimitCheckedStatusProtects against
max_input_tokensbefore each model calltoken_budgetThe quadratic cost of re-sending a growing history (chapter 2): call 20 costs far more than call 2
max_secondsbefore each model calltimeoutA user who has given up long before the budget runs out
max_iterationsbefore each model callmax_iterationsThe simplest backstop on cost and time
max_repeatswhen a reply asks for toolsrepeated_callA model stuck on one failing call, burning its budget for nothing

Three design choices are worth knowing, because they are the ones people get wrong. First, the token and time limits are strict (stop when the total is more than the limit) while the iteration limit is reached (the call after number max_iterations is refused); an off-by-one here is the classic bug, and the checker has a hand case for each. Second, when several limits are exceeded the guard reports one reason, in the order token budget, timeout, iterations, so a log line says the most informative thing first. Third, the repeat key is the tool name plus the input as canonical JSON (sort_keys=True), because a model may reorder the keys of an otherwise identical call.

A deadline needs a clock, and a test that sleeps is slow and flaky. The guard takes any zero-argument function that returns seconds, so tests pass a FakeClock they wind by hand. Step through a run that crosses the token line while time and iterations are still fine:

from starter import Budget, FakeClock, LoopGuard

clock = FakeClock()
guard = LoopGuard(Budget(max_iterations=4, max_input_tokens=3000, max_seconds=20), clock)
for step, (tokens, seconds) in enumerate([(800, 4), (1200, 5), (900, 8), (400, 1)], start=1):
    print(f"before call {step}: {guard.before_model_call()}   (tokens so far {guard.input_tokens}, seconds {clock():g})")
    guard.after_model_call({"input_tokens": tokens, "output_tokens": 50})
    clock.advance(seconds)
print(f"before call 5: {guard.before_model_call()}   (tokens so far {guard.input_tokens}, seconds {clock():g})")
call = {"name": "get_order", "input": {"order_id": "A-1001"}}
guard = LoopGuard(Budget(max_repeats=2), clock)
print([guard.check_calls([call]) for _ in range(3)])
before call 1: None   (tokens so far 0, seconds 0)
before call 2: None   (tokens so far 800, seconds 4)
before call 3: None   (tokens so far 2000, seconds 9)
before call 4: None   (tokens so far 2900, seconds 17)
before call 5: token_budget   (tokens so far 3300, seconds 18)
[None, None, 'repeated_call']

After four calls the guard has used 3,300 tokens against a limit of 3,000, so the fifth call is refused with token_budget even though only 18 of 20 seconds have passed and the iteration limit is also reached. Last line: the third identical call is the first to be reported (max_repeats=2 allows two).

Common misconception

"A repeated call is always a bug." Not always: polling a job's status is legitimate and repeats the same call. max_repeats is a number you tune per deployment, and a better rule for a polling tool is to exempt it by name. The point of the guard is that some rule exists in code, so that a stuck model costs three calls and not three hundred.
milestones.card:
Left alone, a model may call tools forever: it cannot find the answer, or a tool keeps failing. A limit the model is asked to respect is only a request, so the code enforces limits itself, as plain bookkeeping that never calls a model or a tool.

  • Tokens: every model call re-sends the whole history, so call 20 costs far more than call 2.
  • Seconds: the user may give up long before the token budget runs out.
  • Iterations (model calls so far): the simple backstop.
  • Repeats: the same tool with the same input again means the model is stuck.

after_model_call records a finished call, before_model_call returns None or one reason to stop, and check_calls counts requests in self.seen. Key each call by tool name plus its input as JSON with sorted keys, so reordering the keys cannot hide a repeat.

max_iterations=3: the 4th model call is refused
max_input_tokens=100: 100 used is fine, 101 stops the next call
max_repeats=2: the same call a 3rd time gives "repeated_call"

Read more: A4 chapter 2, stopping: the loop must be able to end.

milestones.title: the loop
milestones.task: Write check_pairing(messages), which lists the problems in a history, and agent_loop(...), which runs the loop and returns a RunResult. The six steps of one iteration, the statuses and the answer rules are in the docstring. Leave the trace argument alone until milestone 5.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 4 shows this milestone as ✔. It tests check_pairing on hand-built histories (a missing result, an orphan result, a duplicate, wrong roles, a history that ends on an unanswered call), then runs the chapter 2 conversation, parallel calls, an error and a recovery, each forced stop (the history must stay valid and the answer must be the stop message), a reply cut off by max_tokens, and forty seeded random conversations against an independent validity check.
milestones.explain:
Now the loop itself. Its whole state is the messages list (plus a few counters), which is why it can be checkpointed, replayed in a test and inspected after a failure. That is also why the history must be valid at every exit. A provider rejects a request in which an assistant tool_use is not followed by a user message with a matching tool_result, and a durable agent that resumes from a saved history cannot resume from an invalid one.

One iteration, in the order your code does it:

  1. Ask the guard whether another model call is allowed. If it names a reason, stop with that status.
  2. Call model.complete(messages, system=system, tools=registry.definitions()), tell the guard the usage, and append the reply exactly as received.
  3. No tool requests: the model has answered. Status done, or truncated if the reply was cut off by max_tokens.
  4. Tool requests, but the reply was cut off by max_tokens: the arguments may be incomplete JSON. Do not run them. Answer each with an error result and stop.
  5. Ask the guard about repeats. If it objects, answer every call with an error result ("Not run: ...") and stop with repeated_call.
  6. Otherwise run the calls in order and append one user message with all the results.

Steps 4 and 5 are the interesting ones. They stop the run, so the temptation is to break and return; but then the last assistant message holds tool requests nobody answered. Answering them with an error result costs two lines and keeps the history valid. Running calls in order, one after another, is the safe default for tools with side effects (chapter 2 explains why concurrency needs more thought than a thread pool). Here is the happy path from chapter 2, and then a model that never gives up on the same call:

from llm import ScriptedModel, tool_use
from starter import Shop, agent_loop, check_pairing, make_registry

model = ScriptedModel([
    [tool_use("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}, id="t1")],
    [tool_use("track_shipment", {"carrier": "UPS"}, id="t2")],
    "Order A-1001 shipped with UPS and is out for delivery in Leeds.",
])
r = agent_loop(model, "Where is order A-1001?", make_registry(Shop()), system="You are a support agent.")
print(r.status, "| model calls:", r.iterations, "| input tokens:", r.input_tokens)
print(r.answer)
for i, m in enumerate(r.messages):
    kinds = [m["content"]] if isinstance(m["content"], str) else [b["type"] for b in m["content"]]
    print(f"  message {i}: {m['role']:9s} {kinds}")
print("pairing problems:", check_pairing(r.messages))

stuck = ScriptedModel(lambda messages, tools, system: [tool_use("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"})])
r = agent_loop(stuck, "Where is order A-1001?", make_registry(Shop()))
print("\nstuck model:", r.status, "after", r.iterations, "model calls")
print("answer:", r.answer)
print("last message:", r.messages[-1]["content"][0]["content"])
print("pairing problems:", check_pairing(r.messages))
done | model calls: 3 | input tokens: 1188
Order A-1001 shipped with UPS and is out for delivery in Leeds.
  message 0: user      ['Where is order A-1001?']
  message 1: assistant ['tool_use']
  message 2: user      ['tool_result']
  message 3: assistant ['tool_use']
  message 4: user      ['tool_result']
  message 5: assistant ['text']
pairing problems: []

stuck model: repeated_call after 3 model calls
answer: I stopped because I kept repeating the same tool call without making progress.
last message: Not run: this exact call has been made too many times. Change your approach or explain the problem to the user.
pairing problems: []

The first run uses three model calls and 1,188 input tokens in total, and each call re-sends everything before it. The stuck model is stopped on its third request, the third call is not executed, yet check_pairing finds nothing wrong. That is the property you are building.

Systems connection

The loop is an ordinary service handler, and the guard is its resilience layer: a deadline for the whole task (the budget idea of failure, timeouts and retries), a cap on retries, and a refusal to repeat what has not worked. The "Not run" results are the agent version of failing fast with a clear reason. And when a tool call times out in a real system, the harness cannot tell whether the side effect happened; chapter 5 and Lab 2 show the idempotency key that makes the retry safe.
milestones.card:
The whole state of an agent loop is its list of messages, which is why a run can be saved, replayed and inspected. That only works while the list is valid at every exit: a provider rejects a history in which a tool request from the assistant is not answered by a matching result in the very next user message.

check_pairing(messages) returns the problems, each starting message <index>: and naming the id. agent_loop follows the six steps in its docstring, using LoopGuard and run_tool, and appends reply.as_message() exactly as received. All results for one assistant turn travel in one user message, in call order. The trap is a forced stop: when the guard objects, or a reply was cut off by max_tokens, do not return at once. Answer every pending request with an error result starting "Not run:", then stop, so the history stays valid.

assistant: tool_use a, tool_use b
user:      tool_result a, tool_result b    (one message, same order)
assistant: text only -> status done

Read more: A4 chapter 2, the loop.

milestones.title: logging and reading a trace
milestones.task: Extend your agent_loop so that, when trace is not None, it adds a model_call event after each model call, a tool_call event after each tool run and one stop event at the end. Then write summarise(events). The event fields and the summary keys are in the docstrings.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 5 shows this milestone as ✔. It runs a scripted conversation on a FakeClock (each tool advances the clock by 2.5 seconds, so seconds can be checked exactly), compares the events with the usage the model really reported, checks that every forced stop also ends the trace, tests summarise on hand-written events (including two identical failed calls), and finally diagnoses three misbehaving runs from their traces alone.
milestones.explain:
When an agent run goes wrong, the transcript is the fastest diagnosis, and the same records become your evaluation data later (tracing and observability for LLM systems). The loop already holds all the facts; the job is to record them as structured events, plain dictionaries that a program can count, instead of lines of prose that a person must read. Your loop writes three kinds:

EventWhenFields besides kind
model_callafter each model calli, stop_reason, input_tokens, output_tokens, tools (names requested)
tool_callafter each tool runi, id, tool, input, is_error, result_chars, seconds
stoponce, at the endstatus, iterations

Those are the leaf records of what distributed tracing calls spans: a model call and a tool call are the two kinds of span an agent run is made of. summarise reduces a list of events to the numbers you read first. The one with a definition worth stating is wasted_calls: a tool call that errored, or that repeats an earlier call of the same run with the same input. It is a blunt measure, but it is the first one that separates a model that is confused by your tools from one that is simply slow. The demo runs a model that makes a typo (the letter O for a zero), corrects itself, and then asks for the same order again for no reason:

import json
from llm import ScriptedModel, tool_use
from starter import Shop, Trace, agent_loop, make_registry, summarise

model = ScriptedModel([
    [tool_use("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1OO1"}, id="t1")],              # a typo: letter O instead of zero
    [tool_use("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}, id="t2")],
    [tool_use("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}, id="t3")],              # asks again for no reason
    "Order A-1001 has shipped.",
])
class Tick:                       # a clock that advances 0.05 s every time it is read
    t = 0.0
    def __call__(self):
        self.t = round(self.t + 0.05, 3)
        return self.t

trace = Trace()
agent_loop(model, "Where is order A-1001?", make_registry(Shop()), trace=trace, clock=Tick())
for e in trace.events:
    print(json.dumps(e))
print()
print(json.dumps(summarise(trace.events), indent=1))
{"kind": "model_call", "i": 1, "stop_reason": "tool_use", "input_tokens": 372, "output_tokens": 6, "tools": ["get_order"]}
{"kind": "tool_call", "i": 1, "id": "t1", "tool": "get_order", "input": {"order_id": "A-1OO1"}, "is_error": true, "result_chars": 172, "seconds": 0.05}
{"kind": "model_call", "i": 2, "stop_reason": "tool_use", "input_tokens": 421, "output_tokens": 6, "tools": ["get_order"]}
{"kind": "tool_call", "i": 2, "id": "t2", "tool": "get_order", "input": {"order_id": "A-1001"}, "is_error": false, "result_chars": 60, "seconds": 0.05}
{"kind": "model_call", "i": 3, "stop_reason": "tool_use", "input_tokens": 442, "output_tokens": 6, "tools": ["get_order"]}
{"kind": "tool_call", "i": 3, "id": "t3", "tool": "get_order", "input": {"order_id": "A-1001"}, "is_error": false, "result_chars": 60, "seconds": 0.05}
{"kind": "model_call", "i": 4, "stop_reason": "end_turn", "input_tokens": 463, "output_tokens": 7, "tools": []}
{"kind": "stop", "status": "done", "iterations": 4}

{
 "status": "done",
 "iterations": 4,
 "input_tokens": 1698,
 "output_tokens": 25,
 "tool_calls": 3,
 "errors": 1,
 "calls_by_tool": {
  "get_order": 3
 },
 "wasted_calls": 2,
 "seconds": 0.15
}

Read the summary as a diagnosis. Three tool calls, one error, two wasted: the typo cost one call, and the redundant request cost another. The ids differ in the events but the inputs are identical, which is why the repeat key uses the input and not the id. Lab 2 uses the same idea over twenty tasks, and counts error rate and tokens as the numbers that pick between two tool designs.
milestones.card:
When a run goes wrong, the record of what happened is the fastest way to diagnose it. The loop writes that record as a list of events, plain dictionaries a program can count: one per model call, one per tool call and one at the end. A summary turns the list into the few numbers you read first.

summarise(events) returns a dict with exactly the keys in its docstring, and the loop that writes the events is already in the file. The definition to get right is wasted_calls: a tool call that errored, or that repeats an earlier call of the same run, meaning the same tool with the same input. Each event counts once, even if it is both. Compare inputs, not ids, because a model that repeats itself gets a new id each time. Key each call by tool name plus its input as sorted JSON, as the stopping rules do.

get_order A-1OO1 (error), get_order A-1001, get_order A-1001 (again)
-> tool_calls 3, errors 1, wasted_calls 2

Read more: A4 chapter 2, making the loop safe to run.

milestones.title: the same loop with a text-only model
milestones.task: Write parse_react(reply) (never raises), to_transcript(messages) and ReActModel.complete(...). react_system is given. Run your unchanged agent_loop with ReActModel(ScriptedModel([...strings...])) as the model.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 6 shows this milestone as ✔. It checks parse_react on a dozen hand cases (an invented Observation: is cut off, a reply that invents one before acting is an error, bad JSON, JSON that is not an object, which marker comes first), sixty seeded junk strings that must not raise, the exact transcript text, the adapter alone (ids, retry after a format error, usage summed), and three end-to-end runs: the text model reaches the same answer as the native model with the same tool calls, the second prompt contains the real observation and none of the invented one, and an invalid argument is caught by validate_args and shown to the model as an observation.
milestones.explain:
Chapter 3 introduced ReAct in its original form: the model writes lines of text, Thought: then Action:, and the harness parses the action, runs it and appends an Observation:. Native tool calling replaced the parsing with structured blocks, but a text-only model (a small local model, a base model, a provider with no tool support) still needs the old form. The right way to support it is not a second loop. It is an adapter, so that guards, validation, error results and tracing all keep working.

Three rules make the text format safe, and they are all about who writes the observation. The format is Action: tool_name {"json": "arguments"} on one line. The model must stop after the action line (in a real API, a stop sequence of Observation:; the stand-in model cannot be told to stop, so your parser does it): anything from the first Observation: line on is the model inventing what the tool would have said, and it is discarded. A reply that invents an observation before it has acted has nothing valid left, which is an error, not a free answer. And when the reply cannot be parsed, the model is shown its mistake as a format error and asked again, a limited number of times.

from llm import ScriptedModel
from starter import ReActModel, Shop, agent_loop, make_registry, parse_react

print(parse_react('Thought: I need the order.\nAction: get_order {"order_id": "A-1001"}\nObservation: it shipped via FedEx'))
print(parse_react("Final Answer: It shipped with UPS."))
print(parse_react('Action: get_order {"order_id": }'))

text_model = ScriptedModel([
    'Thought: I need the order first.\nAction: get_order {"order_id": "A-1001"}\nObservation: it shipped via FedEx',
    'Thought: The carrier is in the observation.\nAction: track_shipment {"carrier": "UPS"}',
    "Thought: I have both facts.\nFinal Answer: Order A-1001 shipped with UPS and is out for delivery in Leeds.",
])
result = agent_loop(ReActModel(text_model), "Where is order A-1001?", make_registry(Shop()))
print(result.status, "|", result.answer)
print("--- the prompt the text model saw on its last call ---")
print(text_model.calls[2]["messages"][0]["content"])
{'kind': 'action', 'thought': 'I need the order.', 'tool': 'get_order', 'input': {'order_id': 'A-1001'}}
{'kind': 'final', 'thought': '', 'answer': 'It shipped with UPS.'}

milestones.card:
A text-only model cannot send structured tool calls, so it writes lines of text instead: its reasoning, then the tool to call and the arguments to give it. An adapter translates between that text and the tool-calling format, so the same loop, guards, validation and tracing work unchanged.

The lines are Thought: then Action: tool {json} (the arguments as one JSON object), or Final Answer: when done. parse_react(reply) turns one reply into a dict and never raises. It first cuts the reply at the first line starting Observation:, because anything after that is the model inventing what the tool would say; your code supplies the real one. to_transcript(messages) goes the other way and renders the history as text. ReActModel.complete builds the prompt, calls self.inner with react_system (already written), parses the reply and, on a format error, shows the model its mistake and asks again a limited number of times.
